The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

The following descriptions give the same function $\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$: the power series $\sum x^n/\iota(n!)$; the product limit $\lim_n(1+x/\iota(n))^n$; the normalized solution of $y'=y,\ y(0)=1$; the normalized continuous multiplicative function; and the compact-uniform limit of the Picard iterates.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be the declared probability model for a
pre-specified target population of measurement conditions. Let $A$ and $B$ be
real random variables giving quantitative measurements of the same target
under the same stated conditions. The choice of target population and the
scientific applicability of its probability law are model assumptions; this
definition does not verify them.

Assume the paired difference $D:=A-B$ is square-integrable. It is measurable
because measurable real functions are closed under finite sums and scalar
multiples ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]).
Since $0\le(|D|-1)^2$, we have $|D|\le(D^2+1)/2$. Monotonicity,
homogeneity, and additivity of the nonnegative integral, together with
$\mathbb P(\Omega)=1$, give
$$\mathbb E[|D|]\le\tfrac12\mathbb E[D^2]+\tfrac12<\infty$$
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],
[[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). Thus define the finite
population bias $\mu_D:=\mathbb E[D]$. Put $H:=D-\mu_D$, which is measurable by
the same closure result. Its square $H^2$ is measurable by
[[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]. Since
$$H^2\le 2D^2+2\mu_D^2,$$
monotonicity, homogeneity, and additivity of the nonnegative integral give
$$\mathbb E[H^2]\le 2\mathbb E[D^2]+2\mu_D^2<\infty$$
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],
[[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). Therefore
$$\sigma_D:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(D)}=\sqrt{\mathbb E[H^2]}$$
is a finite real standard deviation, since $\operatorname{Var}(D)=\mathbb E[H^2]$
by [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and every nonnegative real has a
square root by [[thm-of-square-roots]].
The sign convention is $D=A-B$, so positive bias means that $A$ reads larger
than $B$ on average. The conventional rounded normal-reference limits of
agreement are $\mu_D-1.96\sigma_D$ and $\mu_D+1.96\sigma_D$.

For an iid sample $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ of paired differences from the declared
target population, with $n\ge2$ and observed values $d_1,\ldots,d_n$, define
$$\bar d:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i,\qquad s_D:=\sqrt{\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(d_i-\bar d)^2}.$$
The sample plug-in limits are $\bar d\pm1.96s_D$: they substitute the sample
mean and sample standard deviation into the conventional population formula.
They are point estimates; no unbiasedness, consistency, confidence coverage,
or exact finite-sample coverage for either endpoint is asserted here.

Repeated measurements on one target are not iid merely because there are many
recorded pairs. Their within-target dependence must be stated and modeled, for
example with a covariance or random-effects model. When defined, correlation
measures linear association and does not by itself establish agreement. Limits
of agreement describe the distribution of differences; they do not decide
whether those differences are acceptable for a particular use or whether
either method is calibrated to a known truth.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

derivations.claim: AC in [A1] applies to the normal-law construction [F1]. It also supplies countable choice: for any sequence of nonempty sets, apply AC to the family of its values and compose the resulting choice function with the sequence, which is the property in [F3]. Thus the countable-choice hypothesis in [F4] is available. Taking the one-dimensional box with equal endpoints $x=x$ in [F4] gives $\lambda(\{x\})=0$; the density in [F1] is nonnegative measurable by [F2], so [F5] gives $N(0,1)(\{x\})=0$. Thus the standard normal law has no atoms.

For $x<y$, probability subtraction and the density definition give $\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)=N(0,1)((x,y])=\int_{(x,y]}\phi\,d\lambda$. Let $M=\max\{|x|,|y|\}$. Positivity [F6], derivative [F7], and the mean value theorem [F8] show that the exponential is increasing. Hence on $[x,y]$, $\alpha:=e^{-M^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\le\phi(t)\le\beta:=1/\sqrt{2\pi}$, with $\alpha>0$. By [F4, F13], $0<\alpha(y-x)\le\Phi(y)-\Phi(x)\le\beta(y-x)$. Therefore $\Phi$ is strictly increasing and continuous.

By [F9], $\Phi(n)\to1$ and $\Phi(-n)\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. The density is continuous by [F7] and even. On each compact interval below, [F14, F15] identify its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals, using countable choice from step 1.1. For $n>|x|$, substitution $u=-t$ in [F10] gives $\int_{-n}^{-x}\phi(t)\,dt=\int_x^n\phi(u)\,du$. Passing to the tail limits gives $\Phi(-x)=\mathbb P(Z\ge x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. By the no-atom result in step 1.1, $\mathbb P(Z\ge x)=1-\Phi(x)$, so $\Phi(-x)=1-\Phi(x)$ and $\Phi(0)=1/2$.

By step 2.1, choose an integer $b>0$ with $\Phi(b)>.975$, while $\Phi(0)=1/2<.975$. Step 1.2 makes $\Phi$ continuous on the finite closed interval $[0,b]$, so [F12] gives $z\in(0,b)$ with $\Phi(z)=.975$. Strict increase from step 1.2 makes $z$ unique, and step 2.1 gives $\Phi(-z)=.025$. Strict increase makes these the unique lower quantiles at those levels, so $z=z_{.975}$, the set $\{x:\Phi(x)\ge.975\}$ has infimum $z$, and the set $\{x:\Phi(x)\ge.025\}$ has infimum $-z$.

If $\sigma_D>0$, [F1] gives $F_D(x)=\Phi((x-\mu_D)/\sigma_D)$, since $\mu_D+\sigma_D t\le x$ exactly when $t\le(x-\mu_D)/\sigma_D$. The increasing affine change of variable carries the quantiles from step 3.1 to $\mu_D-z_{.975}\sigma_D$ and $\mu_D+z_{.975}\sigma_D$. By [F1] and step 1.1, this affine image of the standard normal law has no atoms. The endpoint CDF values are $.025$ and $.975$, so the closed interval between them has probability $.975-.025=.95$, as stated.

If $\sigma_D=0$, [F1] gives $N(\mu_D,0)=\delta_{\mu_D}$. Its distribution function is $0$ below $\mu_D$ and $1$ at or above $\mu_D$, so both lower quantiles are $\mu_D$ and the singleton has probability $1$. This is exactly the formula in the Statement with $\sigma_D=0$.

risk_review.notes: Read every current step, all fourteen original direct dependencies, both added compact-integral suppliers and the reader/refuter evidence. AC supplies CC for null singletons, Lebesgue boxes and the integral bridge. Density positivity and the alpha/beta interval bounds give strict increase and Lipschitz continuity. The compact reflection has derivative -1 and a continuous integrand; F14/F15 now explicitly transfer Riemann substitution to Lebesgue integrals. Finite probability continuity justifies both tails. pre-specified target population of measurement conditions. Let $A$ and $B$ be

under the same stated conditions. The choice of target population and the

Assume the paired difference $D:=A-B$ is square-integrable. It is measurable

Since $0\le(|D|-1)^2$, we have $|D|\le(D^2+1)/2$. Monotonicity,
homogeneity, and additivity of the nonnegative integral, together with
$\mathbb P(\Omega)=1$, give
$$\mathbb E[|D|]\le\tfrac12\mathbb E[D^2]+\tfrac12<\infty$$
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],

population bias $\mu_D:=\mathbb E[D]$. Put $H:=D-\mu_D$, which is measurable by
the same closure result. Its square $H^2$ is measurable by

monotonicity, homogeneity, and additivity of the nonnegative integral give

([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]],

is a finite real standard deviation, since $\operatorname{Var}(D)=\mathbb E[H^2]$

For an iid sample $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ of paired differences from the declared

The sample plug-in limits are $\bar d\pm1.96s_D$: they substitute the sample

They are point estimates; no unbiasedness, consistency, confidence coverage,

Repeated measurements on one target are not iid merely because there are many

of agreement describe the distribution of differences; they do not decide
whether those differences are acceptable for a particular use or whether
either method is calibrated to a known truth.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
After identifying $(\Omega,w)$ with the full-power-set probability space of
[[thm-finite-probability-spaces-are-exactly-finite-full-power-set-probability-spaces]],
the expectation defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] agrees with
the published finite formulas:
$$\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)=\sum_{x\in X(\Omega)}x\,\mathbb P(X=x).$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $\mathbb E[A]=1/2$ and $\mathbb E[B]=1/2+c$. Directly summing the two centered squares gives $\operatorname{Var}(A)=\operatorname{Var}(B)=1/4$. By [F4], $\operatorname{Cov}(A,B)=\operatorname{Cov}(A,A+c)=\operatorname{Var}(A)+\operatorname{Cov}(A,c)=1/4$, since covariance with a constant is zero. Thus the denominator in the definition of correlation is $1/4$ and $\operatorname{Corr}(A,B)=1$.
At both points $D=A-B=-c$, so by [F2] and [F3], $\mathbb E[D]=-c$ and $\operatorname{Var}(D)=0$. Hence its conventional limits are $-c\pm1.96\cdot0=(-c,-c)$, while its bias is nonzero.
Therefore perfect correlation does not imply zero bias or interchangeable measurements; any practical tolerance must be supplied for the intended use.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,w)$ be a finite probability space and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$.
After identifying $(\Omega,w)$ with the full-power-set probability space of
[[thm-finite-probability-spaces-are-exactly-finite-full-power-set-probability-spaces]],
the expectation defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] agrees with
the published finite formulas:
$$\mathbb E[X]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega)=\sum_{x\in X(\Omega)}x\,\mathbb P(X=x).$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(Y_j)_{j\in J}$ be finite families of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space. Then covariance is symmetric, and for real scalars $a_i,b_j$,
$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$
This includes empty sums and constant summands. On a finite probability space all real random variables are square-integrable, so the original finite-space case is included with the same centered-product covariance.

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent square-integrable real random variables, then
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.$$

Thus independence implies zero covariance. The converse is false in general.

derivations.claim: Each triple has mass $1/8=(1/2)^3$, so for arbitrary subsets $S_1,S_2,S_3\subseteq\{-1,1\}$, $\mathbb P(U\in S_1,\epsilon_1\in S_2,\epsilon_2\in S_3)=\prod_{j=1}^3 |S_j|/2$. Thus [F1] makes the coordinates independent. Each coordinate has mean $0$ and variance $1$ by the finite weighted sum [F3] and centered-square definition [F4].

By [F5] and [F6], $\mathbb E[D_j]=0$, $\operatorname{Var}(D_j)=\operatorname{Var}(U)+\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_j)+2\operatorname{Cov}(U,\epsilon_j)=2$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(D_1,D_2)=\operatorname{Var}(U)=1$; all cross terms vanish because they are covariances of distinct independent coordinates.

The event $D_1=D_2=2$ requires the single triple $(1,1,1)$, so its probability is $1/8$. Each event $D_j=2$ requires $U=1$ and $\epsilon_j=1$ and has probability $1/4$, making the product of marginal probabilities $1/16$. The factorization required for independence therefore fails; by [F2] the two differences are not iid.
